title: Gradient normals and tangent directions
section: Directional Derivatives and the Gradient ▷ Normals to Level Sets
terms: normal to a level set; tangent vector; normal line; intersection of level surfaces.

exposition.text:
1
If f is C and ∇f(P ) ̸= 0, its gradient is normal to the regular level set through P . Every
tangent vector v satisfies ∇f (P) · v = 0. The normal line is P + t∇f(P ), and the tangent plane
to a level surface is ∇f(P ) · (x − P ) = 0.
For the intersection of two regular level surfaces f = c and g = d, independent gradients give
the tangent direction ∇f × ∇g. At a critical point with vanishing gradient the normal equation
becomes vacuous, so the surface must be analyzed separately. A tangent direction need not
remain on the curved surface as a straight line; it describes only first-order motion.

question.text:
2 2 2
At (1, 1, 1), which vector is tangent to the curve where x + y + z = 3 and x + 2y + 3z = 6
intersect?
(A) (1, 1, −2) (B) (1, −2, 1) (C) (2, −1, −1) (D) (1, 0, −1) (E) (0, 3, −2)

solution.text:
The normals are (2, 2, 2) and (1, 2, 3). Their cross product is (2, −4, 2), so (1, −2, 1) is a
tangent direction.

question.text:
2 2 2
At P = (1, 1, 1), consider unit tangent directions to x + y + z = 3. What is the maximum
directional derivative of f = x − y + 2z among these directions?
q
√ √
(A) 2 (B) 2 (C) 14/3 (D) 6 (E) 3

solution.text:
The tangent directions are orthogonal to n = (1, 1, 1). Project ∇f = (1, −1, 2) onto that
plane: subtract (2/3)n. The squared projected norm is 6 − 4/3 = 14/3, which is the maxi-
mum squared rate.

question.text:
2
The normal line to xy + z = 5 at (1, 1, 2) meets z = 0 at (a, b, 0). What is a + b?
(A) −1 (B) 0 (C) 1 (D) 2 (E) 3

solution.text:
The gradient is (y, x, 2z) = (1, 1, 4). The normal line is (1 + t, 1 + t, 2 + 4t), so t = −1/2 at
z = 0. It meets that plane at (1/2, 1/2, 0), giving sum 1.

question.text:
2 2 2
Which describes x + y − z = 0 at the origin?
(A) A regular surface with tangent plane z = 0
(B) A regular surface with tangent plane x + y − z = 0
(C) A surface with a unique normal line parallel to the z-axis
(D) A cone vertex with no single tangent plane in the usual smooth-surface sense
(E) An isolated point of the surface

solution.text:
The gradient vanishes, so its normal equation gives only 0 = 0. The surface contains lines
through the origin in the three independent directions (1, 0, 1), (0, 1, 1), and (1, 0, −1). A
tangent plane would have to contain all three, which no plane can do. Direct geometry, not
the vacuous gradient equation, settles the singularity.
